title: Learning style quiz: visual, auditory, reading or hands-on? Free test — cv.cm
description: Free learning style quiz: rate 16 statements to see whether you prefer to learn visually, by listening, by reading and writing, or hands-on, with study tips for each. No sign-up.
lede: Do you remember diagrams, conversations, notes or things you've tried yourself? Rate 16 statements to see which way of taking in information you prefer, and how to use all four when you study.
about: Learning style models sort people by how they prefer to take in information. A well-known version, Neil Fleming's VARK, uses four: visual (pictures, diagrams, charts), auditory (listening and talking), reading and writing (text, lists, notes) and kinesthetic (doing, examples and practice). This quiz uses the same four preferences.

The statements were written for cv.cm; this is not the VARK questionnaire and has no link to its authors. Research has found little evidence that people learn better when teaching is matched to their preferred style, so treat your result as a preference, not a limit. Most people learn best by mixing methods, and testing yourself and spacing out study sessions help whatever your style.

faq.q: What are the four learning styles?
faq.a: Visual (diagrams, charts and color), auditory (lectures, discussion and saying things out loud), reading and writing (text, lists and notes) and kinesthetic (hands-on practice, real examples and movement).

People do have preferences, and this quiz measures them. What research does not support is the idea that you only learn well in your style. The material matters too: maps are best seen and languages are best heard and spoken.

faq.q: Can I have more than one learning style?
faq.a: Yes. Many people score highly on two or three. Your result names your strongest preference and shows your score for all four.

faq.q: How should I study for my learning style?
faq.a: Start with your preferred method to make material feel approachable, then add others. Whatever your result, quizzing yourself, explaining ideas in your own words and spreading study over several days work better than rereading.

items: A diagram or chart helps me understand something faster than an explanation.
I understand things better when someone talks me through them.
I learn best by reading about a topic in detail.
I understand something best once I've tried it myself.
I remember faces and places better than names.
I remember what people said better than what I read.
Writing notes in my own words helps me remember.
I find it hard to sit still and just listen for a long time.
I use colors, highlighting or mind maps when I study.
Reading aloud or talking it through helps me learn.
I prefer written instructions to a demonstration.
I'd rather jump in and figure things out than read the manual.
When giving directions, I'd rather draw a map than describe the way.
I like podcasts, audiobooks and discussions as ways to learn.
I like lists, headings and handouts I can come back to.
Real examples, experiments and practice make ideas stick for me.

visual.name: Visual learner
visual.body: You think in pictures. Diagrams, charts, maps and color help you see how ideas fit together. Try turning notes into mind maps or flowcharts, watching demonstrations, and sketching a problem before you solve it. Add self-testing so the pictures turn into recall.

auditory.name: Auditory learner
auditory.body: You learn by listening and talking. Lectures, discussion and explaining things out loud help ideas stick. Try study groups, recording key points and playing them back, or teaching a topic to a friend. Write a short summary afterward so you have something to review.

reading.name: Reading and writing learner
reading.body: Words on the page work best for you. You like detailed texts, lists and well-organized notes. Rewrite notes in your own words, turn headings into questions, and make summary sheets. Mix in diagrams or practice problems for topics that are hard to put into words.

kinesthetic.name: Hands-on (kinesthetic) learner
kinesthetic.body: You learn by doing. Practice, real examples, experiments and movement make ideas click. Try worked problems, building models, role play or studying on your feet in short sessions. Connect each idea to something you've experienced, then test yourself on it.
